claims.statement: Population-based analysis of US CDC linked birth–infant death records from 2014 to 2021.
claims.quote: We conducted a retrospective, population-based incidence study using the US CDC linked birth–infant death records from 2014 to 2021, encompassing live births and infant deaths across the United States and US territories [8].

claims.statement: SUID was defined using ICD-10 codes R95, R99, and W75, excluding deaths in the first postnatal week.
claims.quote: SUID cases were identified by underlying cause-of-death ICD-10 codes R95 (Sudden Infant Death Syndrome [SIDS]), W75 (Accidental suffocation and strangulation in bed), and R99 (Other ill-defined and unspecified causes of mortality). Deaths occurring during the first seven postnatal days were excluded to focus on postperinatal vulnerability beyond the first postnatal week.

claims.statement: Postconceptional age (PCA) was defined in weeks as gestational age at birth plus postnatal age at death and served as the primary developmental time scale.
claims.quote: PCA was defined in weeks as gestational age at birth plus postnatal age at death and served as the primary developmental time scale.

claims.statement: Weekly SUID counts across PCA weeks 36 to 90 were modelled using a negative binomial generalised additive model with spline smooths and an offset based on national live-birth proportions.
claims.quote: Weekly SUID counts across PCA weeks 36 to 90 were modelled using a negative binomial generalised additive model with spline smooths and an offset based on national live-birth proportions.

claims.statement: Prespecified negative binomial models compared an early rising window (36–42 PCA weeks) and a late declining window (≥47 PCA weeks).
claims.quote: prespecified negative binomial models compared an early rising window (36–42 PCA weeks) and a late declining window (≥47 PCA weeks).

claims.statement: Among 23,686 eligible SUID cases, PCA-aligned incidence revealed a clear rise, peak, and decline pattern.
claims.quote: Among 23,686 eligible SUID cases, PCA-aligned incidence revealed a clear rise, peak, and decline pattern.

claims.statement: Male and female trajectories overlapped during the rising phase and peak. Sex divergence emerged only after the peak, with persistently higher male incidence during the declining phase.
claims.quote: Male and female rates overlapped early but diverged after the peak, with higher male incidence throughout the declining phase (Figure 2B).

claims.statement: Confirmatory models showed similar male and female incidence in the early window and higher male incidence in the late window.
claims.quote: In the early window, male incidence was similar to female incidence (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 1.14, 95% CI 0.85–1.53; Figure 4A; Supplemental Table 1). In the late window, male incidence exceeded female incidence (IRR 1.36, 95% CI 1.29–1.42; Figure 4B; Supplemental Table 4).

claims.statement: Negative binomial models quantified this transition (figure 4).
claims.quote: negative binomial models quantified this transition (figure 4).

claims.statement: Incidence rate ratios from negative binomial models were fitted separately in early (36–42 PCA weeks) and late (≥47 PCA weeks) developmental windows.
claims.quote: Incidence rate ratios from negative binomial models across developmental windows. Models include PCA (per week), sex, maternal smoking, preterm birth, and prespecified interaction terms.

claims.statement: The study used a population incidence design to estimate the risk of sudden unexpected infant death syndrome (SUID) across different developmental windows.
claims.quote: Incidence rate ratios from negative binomial models across developmental windows. Models include PCA (per week), sex, maternal smoking, preterm birth, and prespecified interaction terms.
